archetype.name: Pretender (goaltending-propped)
archetype.definition: A near-.500 team whose record runs ahead of bottom-five 5-on-5 play, held up by goalies saving well above expected and by a weak Pacific Division around it.

report.headline: Goalies and a soft division hide one of the league's worst 5-on-5 teams
report.take:
San Jose sits fifth in the Pacific at 10-11-2, 21st on the site's Teams tab, and it would be easy to read that as a team taking a step. The underlying numbers say otherwise. The Sharks own 43.4% of the expected goals at 5-on-5, 29th in the league, and 47% of the shot attempts, 27th. They give up 30.5 shots a game, 30th, against a league average of 27.1. Their Goal Diff / GP of -0.78 ranks 27th. This is a team that spends most of its night defending.

What keeps the record respectable is the crease. A year ago San Jose's goalies were 25.7 goals below expected. This season they are 9.5 above, sixth in the league. Both goalies are positive: Alex Nedeljkovic at 6.6 GSAx in 8 starts and Yaroslav Askarov at 3.6 in 15. That earns the B+ goaltending grade, the best of the three groups. Add Pts vs Goal Diff of 2.1, also sixth, and you have a team that has banked more standings points than its play warrants, the same pattern as last season's 86-point year, which also ran well ahead of its goal differential.

The numbers also hide something working the other way. The skaters shoot 9.4% against a league 11.4%, 28th, and 5-on-5 PDO is 98.3. Some of that should come back. The catch is that the forward group grades D+, and Macklin Celebrini carries nearly all of it. He has 27 points in 21 games, sits 17th of 240 centers, and is the only regular forward with an xGF % above 50 (51.8%). Every other forward on the list is in the 37-47% range. Better shooting luck will add goals, but this lineup doesn't have the depth to turn possession around.

So the outlook is mixed. The recent 3-1-1 run looks better than it was, because two of those wins came in overtime and the goals allowed stayed above three a game. The 82-game pace of 78 points depends on the goaltending holding near its current level. If it slips back toward average while the shot share stays where it is, the Sharks drift down the standings. Their division neighbours Los Angeles and Vancouver are struggling badly, which keeps San Jose out of the Pacific basement, but it doesn't make the Sharks a playoff team.

strengths.title: Goaltending saving goals above expected
strengths.body: The Goalies GSAx of 9.5 ranks sixth, and both netminders are positive, with Nedeljkovic's 6.6 in only 8 starts leading the way. That is a complete turnaround from last season's -25.7, and it explains why a team allowing 30-plus shots a game ranks only 15th in save % instead of near the bottom. Some regression is likely, because goaltending this far above a team's own history rarely holds for a full season.

strengths.title: Celebrini drives the offense
strengths.body: Celebrini has 27 points in 21 games while playing over 23 minutes a night. His 51.8% xGF is the only figure among the regular forwards that wins its minutes. He ranks 17th of 240 centers, which makes him the one genuinely good-for-the-league piece up front. His production is real, but the D+ forward grade shows how little support he has.

strengths.title: Shooting luck has room to rebound
strengths.body: The skaters are converting 9.4% of their shots, 28th and two points below the league, even though they put up a league-average 27.6 shots a game. That depressed rate is part of why they score only 2.74 a game. Some recovery is likely, although a D+ forward group probably settles below the league norm rather than at it.

concerns.title: Getting badly out-chanced at 5-on-5
concerns.body: An xGF % of 43.4 (29th) and 30.5 shots against a game (30th) describe a team without the puck. That is a slide from last season's 47.6% xGF and almost back to the 2024-25 level of 43.7%, when the club finished last. Of everything here, this is the most stable signal and the one most likely to decide the season.

concerns.title: Record leaning on close-game points
concerns.body: A Pts vs Goal Diff of 2.1 ranks sixth, which means the standings flatter a -18 goal differential. Three of the last ten games were wins or points earned past regulation. Last season showed the same habit at 6.1, so it may partly be how this team plays, but it is not a foundation to count on.

concerns.title: Wingers and special teams leak
concerns.body: Opposing wingers produce 3.74 points a game against San Jose, 0.7 above their own norms, which ranks 28th. Both special-teams units sit below the league, with the PP at 19.5% (24th) and the PK at 74.7% (21st). There is no edge on either unit to make up for the even-strength deficit.

trend.note: The Sharks played October near .500, then a five-game losing streak around the turn of the month dragged them under. A 3-1-1 run over the last five games has steadied the record, but two of those wins needed overtime.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games: two winnable, then the league's stingiest defense
weekAhead.body:
All three games are at home. Calgary and Seattle are both ranked below San Jose on the site (26th and 29th), and both share the Sharks' problem of being out-chanced at 5-on-5. Calgary beat San Jose 2-1 here on Nov. 2. The Flames' -1.1 Goal Diff / GP is worse than San Jose's, but their power play converts 27.1% (5th), and the Sharks' PK is a weak spot. Seattle is the softer target. The Kraken own the league's worst shot-attempt share at 41%, kill only 62.7% of penalties, and allow 7.72 points a game to forwards. Their 103 PDO suggests they have been running hot.

Minnesota closes the week and is a different class. The Wild are 15-3-4, second on the site, first in goals allowed and first in GSAx (15.9). They hold forwards to 4.27 points a game, the fewest in the league, and they beat San Jose 4-1 earlier this month. A good week means four points from the first two games. Anything taken off Minnesota is a bonus.

keyMatchups.title: Sharks PP against Seattle's PK
keyMatchups.body: Seattle's 62.7% penalty kill ranks 31st, and its defense allows centers 0.66 points a game above their norms (30th). That gives Celebrini and Will Smith their best opening of the week. San Jose's PP has been below average at 19.5%, so this is the game where it has to cash in.

keyMatchups.title: Calgary's power play against the PK
keyMatchups.body: The Flames score just 2-ish goals' worth at even strength, with a 9% shooting rate (31st), but their PP sits fifth at 27.1%. Against San Jose's 21st-ranked kill, staying out of the box is the clearest path to beating a team that scores little otherwise.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota's goaltending wall
keyMatchups.body: The Wild lead the league with a .917 save % and 15.9 GSAx. A Sharks team already shooting 9.4% is unlikely to out-finish them. San Jose's own goaltending would have to steal this one.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Sharks win their 5-on-5 minutes against Calgary and Seattle, two teams that also get out-chanced. If they can't tilt the ice against these opponents, the recent 3-1-1 is goaltending and overtime, not progress.

restOfSeason.body:
The current pace is 78 points, and that assumes the goaltending and close-game results keep cooperating. The shot share is the durable number, and at 43.4% xGF it describes a bottom-five team. The 9.5 GSAx is the most fragile piece, since it is far above last season and probably regresses toward average. The low shooting percentage should partly recover, which offsets some of that. Net, I expect a slight drift down from the pace, to something like 70-78 points.

The division softens the fall: Los Angeles and Vancouver below them are struggling badly. Still, with the Oilers and Golden Knights well clear, a playoff spot would require the underlying play to change, not just the bounces. Celebrini's level is real and sets a floor on the offense. The rest of the forward group grades D+, and that will cap it.
swingFactors: Whether Nedeljkovic and Askarov keep saving goals above expected
Celebrini's health and the depth forwards' shooting luck

confidence.note: Only 23 games played, but the shot-share and goaltending signals are strong and consistent with team history.
